utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And good morning to everyone. Before I take the appearances as usual, it has been decided that the delay caused by the IT problems today means that having resumed at this hour we will sit until 11.50 and then take a 25 minute break and sit for 90 minutes from 12.15 to 1.45. Yes, may I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm Tom Hannis, with our Case Manager, Crispian Smith. And I would like to raise two or three procedural or administrative matters before we have the witness in, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning, thank you -- and, yes, Mr. Bajagic is also here. I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honours, for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first matter concerns a matter that's been pending before Your Honours, it's confidential, it regards the issuance of a subpoena for a witness who is scheduled to appear next year in January. Because of some difficulties in getting the paperwork resolved, we wanted to change the appearance date set forth in that subpoena from the 25th of January to the 28th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You are now moving for that amendment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. No, there shouldn't be any difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The second matter relates to this witness. Mr. Nielsen, when I spoke with him on Sunday before he testified, he'd made a request of me if he could obtain an electronic copy of the B/C/S transcript of Mr. Stanisic's suspect interview. He already has received DVDs that are the video of that interview, but he indicated in listening to the video, he is not sure about what is said in some of the B/C/S. He has an English transcript, but he doesn't have the B/C/S transcript. I was unable to give that to him before he began testifying. I would like to provide it to him, but now that he is sworn as a witness, I'm nervous about violating any rule about contacting the witness, and so I wanted to bring that to Defence counsel's attention and your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Give it to us and we'll give it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's what I was going to propose. And the third matter relates to the tendering of some documents with Mr. Nielsen. There are about four documents that I showed him yesterday which are not in his report and not already on the witness -- not already on the exhibit list, and I would like to tender those separately because we will be giving a list to the Registry of the documents in his report that are on our 65 ter list and we want to tender, but these should be identified separately because they are not in his report. And I can name those now or at the end of his testimony, whatever is more convenient for the Court and the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you are speaking to Mr. Hannis's last?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, well, the previous and the last. I must say that I'm a bit concerned with the fact that the witness has been provided with the interview of one of the suspects. I mean, if -- my understanding is that the expert witness should be pretty neutral in the proceedings in order to be able to give a neutral expert opinion. Now, the fact being that he has already been disclosed with the English and the video, makes my objection to provide the Serbian copy moot, so to speak. But I just wanted to raise my concern with that. As concerning the last matter which Mr. Hannis raised, if I correctly understand these four documents are on the 65 ter list? In this case, we don't have any objections. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In terms of -- Mr. Hannis, in terms of your request to -- I'm not sure that you phrased it as such, but this question of providing the audio version of the interview to the expert witness, we all in a sense shared the surprise articulated by Mr. Zecevic, but on the other hand, recognising the witness's status as an expert and without putting you on the spot as to -- in terms of asking whether this is peculiar to this case and this witness, we see no objection to your so providing him with the audio transcript in as much as Mr. Zecevic says he has the other -- the video version already. In terms of your -- the matter of the additional exhibits, additional items to be tendered through the witness, you may so proceed. The Defence raising no objection, these items all being on your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me deal with that first, and I'll come back to the suspect interview. The 65 ter numbers for the documents I wanted to tender now are 2368, 2370, 2371, and 2372. These were appointments made on May 15th by Mr. Stanisic of Mr. Bjelosevic, Mr. Jesuric, Mr. Karisik, and Mr. Zupljanin as members of that staff for command and control of MUP war units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I was waiting to see if an exhibit number would be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The following documents will be assigned the respective exhibit numbers: 65 ter 2368 shall be Exhibit P455; 65 ter 2370 shall be Exhibit P456; 65 ter 2371 shall be Exhibit P457; and 65 ter 2372 shall be Exhibit P458. I think I have one more left. 65 ter 2371 shall be Exhibit P459. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter P42372 shall be Exhibit P457 -- no? Yes. Let me take that again, please. 65 ter 2368 shall be Exhibit P455; 65 ter 2370 shall be Exhibit P456; 65 ter 2371 shall be Exhibit P457; and 65 ter 2372 shall be Exhibit P458. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to the matter of the suspect interview, just to clarify, the expert witness previously had received from us the video version, which includes audio, the video and audio version of the suspect interview. He also has a copy of the written transcript in English, and he had requested from me on Sunday a copy of the transcript in B/C/S because he indicated in reading the English transcript and listening to the audio sometimes there were portions in the English that were listed as inaudible but he believed he could hear them, and he wanted to see if the B/C/S transcript was substantially or maybe more reflective of what was actually said than the English version. And as regard your surprise and Mr. Zecevic's surprise about the fact that he had received it at all, I will have to tell you internally we had a discussion about whether or not we should provide it to him. Based on my experience with expert witnesses in my home jurisdiction, often times one of the first questions from a Defence attorney examining an expert in a situation like this would be: Well, have you seen or read the interview of my client in a situation like this. So we thought, well, is it better for him to read it or not. In the end we decided, well, we should give him the opportunity and then he can decide whether he wants to read it or not and deal with questions about it as they come up. That was how we decided. I seem to recall in one of the other cases here that I worked on that we did provide -- well, in one case I know the suspect interview was performed by the person who turned out to be the Prosecution's expert. It was a military general in the Milutinovic case. He was interviewed, in part, by Mr. Coo who was proposed as a Defence expert, although in the end he didn't -- wasn't allowed to testify as an expert, in part because of the fact that he participated in the interview, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Bench is not allowing you to provide anything you already provided the witness with. We are only assisting you in the problem of communicating with the witness which during his testimony you can't [realtime transcript read in error "can"] do. Okay. That's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all I'm requesting. Thank you. And with that I'm ready to have the witness come back in. And what we propose to do is give that transcript to the Registry officer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For the transcript, line -- page 6, line 9 is -- it should be can't -- "cannot do" and not "can do." Cannot do, "which during his testimony you cannot do." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Nielsen. I remind you that you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Dr. Nielsen. I apologise for the delay. We've had technical difficulties this morning. Before I return to the MUP annual report, which is at tab 80 in your binder, and which is 65 ter number 279, I wanted to ask you two or three general questions about subordination or resubordination of the police. In your review of the documents, did you come across any documents dealing with or describing resubordination of police units to the military? Did you find any document, for example, that was a decision or an order saying that a particular police unit or units were going to be subordinated or resubordinated to the army for combat purposes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen a number of such orders throughout the period of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are those military orders or police orders?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't call all of those documents necessarily orders. "Orders" refers to a particular kind of document, of course. What I have seen are documents including orders but also including reports from the field, that is to say, progress reports or status reports as well as cumulative reports, such as the RS MUP draft annual report, and quarterly, semi annual, and annual reports at the regional and municipal level that clearly state that there were circumstances particularly for combat purposes in which police units were subordinated to the command of the Army of Republika Srpska. Those documents, of course the majority of documents I've reviewed are police documents. However, I have also seen a number of military documents that refer to such subordination from the VRS's point of view, and my attention was directed to such documents by my colleagues who were analysts in the military analysis unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the event police were resubordinated, did military police enforce discipline and make arrest of police members in the event that violations of either the law or military discipline occurred?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were incidents in which police members were indeed arrested by members of the military. I have reviewed documents in which that was the case. I would point out that the matter of who, as it were, had the power or authority to arrest whom, was a matter of ongoing debate and discussion between the RS MUP and the VRS. This is reflected consistently in police documents, in military documents that I have reviewed, and it is most certainly reflected in the 11 July 1992 meeting that took place in Belgrade and to which I referred yesterday. It is referred to in the 17 July 1992 document that was disseminated by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the RS pursuant to the conclusions of the 11 July 1992 meeting, and I would like to highlight that one of the conclusions was namely that the top hierarchy of both the army and the MUP needed to meet as soon as possible to discuss a whole array of issues that were emerging in the context of their joint operations. The general findings that I've been able to reach or that I was able to reach when I was drafting this report on the relationship between the RS MUP and the VRS are set out in pages 72 to 74 of my report, and I would point out that resubordination again is consistently taking place within the context of the 15 May 1992 order that was issued by the minister, and which we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the example of Manjaca camp, which was, as I understand it, a police camp, but guards were provided -- was a military camp but guards were provided by the police. Who had the authority or ability to discipline police guards at Manjaca, was that the army or the police or both?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also understand that Manjaca was -- for the duration of its existence a military and not a police facility. As I mentioned yesterday, the police did indeed take part in the guarding of the facility at certain points during the summer of 1992, and that this was a point of contention between the police and the military. And with respect to who had the authority to discipline police guards if such discipline were meted out, it is my understanding that police officers performing duties that were not in combat zones or in combat activities, and certainly guard duties at a military facility would not be normally defined as combat activities, that they would most likely - this is again my understanding - be subject to discipline according to police procedures and not to army procedures if I such proceedings were initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And one last question regarding the police and the army. In the municipalities at that level where we are talking about Municipal Crisis Staffs, did you see any documents reflecting police being subordinated to the police -- being subordinated to the army at the direction of the politicians in the Crisis Staff, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe the Court has been informed by the expert on Crisis Staffs, and I concur with her findings based on my analysis of police documents and Crisis Staff documents pertaining to the police, it is extremely difficult from an analytical point of view to generalise by the use of police by the Crisis Staffs because so much of what was done was contingent upon the particular circumstances obtaining in a given municipality or region. However, I can certainly state that I have seen documents during the -- my review of MUP and Crisis Staff documents pertaining to the MUP that indicate that there were situations, cases, in which the Crisis Staff leadership, and I remind the Court that the Crisis Staff leadership included at the municipal level as a rule of thumb the chief of the municipal public security station as well as representatives of the political and military leadership in that municipality, in which it was suggested, I don't know if I've -- I can say that it was ordered, but it was certainly suggested and discussed frequently that the police and the military would be conducting joint operations on the territory of that or neighbouring municipalities in order to put down what was viewed by Bosnian Serb officials as an attempted armed uprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to return to the RS MUP annual report. That's 65 ter 279. Tab 80 in your binder. And first look at page 8 of the English, and I think that's page 11 of the B/C/S in e-court. Yes. Looking in the middle of the page in the English, it's -- the paragraph reads: "In addition to other measures, pursuant to a request by the organs of authority, the Security Services Centres and police stations placed 6.176 police officers, mainly from the reserve force, at the disposal of the army. This was a considerable help in combat activities against the enemy." First of all, my question is, the reference to a request by organs, by the organs of authority, can you tell us who or what that is referring to in this context?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it to be a reference to most likely the Presidency the RS and perhaps also the government of the RS where precisely this issue was discussed at meetings of both bodies during the summer of 1992. It probably also refers to the aforementioned joint meetings of the VRS and the RS MUP pursuant to discussions and orders that took place at the Presidency of the RS and at the government of the RS on the issue of personnel and on the issue of joint operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last sentence in the paragraph, maybe you can help clarify for me. It reads in the translation: "Although they did not take personal part in combat, it should be stressed that the members of the police helped the Army of Republika Srpska by capturing, pursuant to a request by military authorities, 2.484 and bringing in 6.985 draft Dodgers." First of all, if you can read the B/C/S, is that an accurate translation of what's written in the original?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that to be a fairly accurate translation of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In the sentence where it says "they did not take personal part in combat," who is the "they" referring to, is that the 6.176 police officers mentioned right above? Or can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that certainly there's room for a bit of ambiguity here in the document. When we have a personal pronoun such as "they" it usually refers to the previous plural noun that's mentioned in the context of that paragraph, so, yes, it does seem to be a reference to those 6.167 [sic] police officers, most of whom stem from the reserve staff. I would point out that whatever "they" refers to here in this particular document, it is absolutely the case that there were a number of instances in which the police assisted the VRS in finding persons to whom they referred as draft dodgers, persons who were of military age and eligibility, conscripts as it were, but who were avoiding, for whatever reason, military duty, and it may also be as this paragraph seems to suggest, that some of the police that were, as a result of requests of higher organs, moved or put at the disposition of the VRS participated in such actions. However, it also seems if we look at the sentence that this was a considerable help in combat activities against the enemy. There's obviously two possible ways of reading that. Did they, themselves, participate in combat activity, or was their help in combat activity provided in the way that they helped the VRS get up to full strength by identifying these draft dodgers, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you shed any light on the two numbers, the 2.484 and the and the number of draft dodgers? That 2.484 appears to be a different number or a different group than draft Dodger?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, this is a good point now that I'm looking closer at it. I mean, I read the B/C/S to say that they -- they caught 2.484 persons and that they brought over 6.985 military draft dodgers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like next to go to page 19 of the English. And it's page 27 of the B/C/S. Top of the page in B/C/S and near the top in English. Paragraph reads: "In this period, police stations provided help to state organs in the implementation of certain measures (the so-called 'assistance') in 2350 cases. Apart from this, they helped and in the beginning independently provided security for some of the collection centres. (530 police officers were engaged in these tasks.)" First of all, in the context of this paragraph, do you know what "assistance" in closed quotes refers to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And 530 police officers, I take it from this sentence means that they were -- providing security means they were guarding people at collection centres?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that they secured certain collective centres, yes, so I take that to be another way of saying that they were guarding these centres, and I would point out that, as I noted yesterday, the use of police personnel to guard collective centres was a point of contention within the RS MUP and it was one of the activities which the RS MUP certainly, after 11 July 1992, increasingly sought to divest itself of; that is, they sought to get out of the business, as it were, of guarding detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your report, you talk in some detail about this annual report, so I'm just going to ask you a couple of more points that aren't referred to specifically in your report. The next one is at page 23 of the English and that's page 32 of the B/C/S. Near the bottom in B/C/S, near the top in English. It has to do with communications. This is under the section on reporting and informing. You see second paragraph on the English page: "On average 15 dispatches a day were sent to the centres and other organs of the interior from the MUP headquarters and on average 16 dispatches a day were received." "... other organs of the interior," what does that refer to in this context?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read this as referring the centres -- refer to the centres for public -- excuse me, the Security Services Centres, that is, the regional organs of the MUP, and "other organs" I would read as including, amongst other things, the public security stations at the municipal level. It could also include, and I believe did include, the border police, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you just mentioned the centres for security services, you used the term "services" in the plural. Can you tell us what that refers to with regard to the centres?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbian acronym CSB is correctly translated as Security Services, plural, Centre. That is to say, the CSB is a unit, organisational unit within the Ministry of Internal Affairs, in which there are both tasks of public security and state security, or as it was called after April 1992 in the RS, national security. In other words, at the CSB level, at the level of the chief of the CSB, the two branches, the two main services of Internal Affairs in the RS public security and national security come together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were the chiefs or the heads of the CSBs, did they have authority over both public and National Security Services?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to both the 1990 rule book of SR BiH MUP on the internal organisation of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, as well as the subsequent draft 1992 rule book on internal organisation of the RS Ministry of Internal Affairs, it can be seen that the chief of regional Security Services Centres continued to have a role vis-a-vis both public and National Security Services.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly, if we could go to page 28 of the English, and page 39 of the B/C/S. The bottom half of the page for both. This is the section on organisation, systemisation, and personal status. You see there's a brief paragraph about the transformation of the Special Police units having been carried out which reduced local influence on the use of these units. I think that's something that you've talked about before. And then near the -- well, at the very bottom of the B/C/S page and in the list of bullet points above item number 5, you'll see the third bullet point says, "a draft decision determining which MUP employees are considered as authorised officials." This is among the list of things that have been done and compiled during this reporting period. Do you know what that draft decision was and what it said regarding which MUP employees were considered as authorised officials?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that draft decision. It's not a document that I believe I was able to review. I certainly do not recall having seen it. I think it is important to point out here that there were a number, a considerable number of items in RS MUP's organisation and indeed its definitions of tasks, functions, duties, et cetera, that were being considered during the course of 1992 for redrafting where we see again at the 11 July 1992 meeting, the heads of CSBs, the minister himself, making suggestions as to how the RS MUP could function better if certain internal documents, the rule book, definitions of authorised officials and other matters were redefined or better defined to suit the extraordinary circumstances in which the RS MUP was operating from April 1992 forwards. We also have to remember that with all the documents, as I show in my report with reference to the RS law and Internal Affairs and the RA MUP rule book on internal organisation, they operated on the basis initially of the documents that they have -- had, of course, all known and operated according to previously in SR BiH MUP, but obviously now that they had their own Ministry of Internal Affairs and they had increased freedom to construct and structure that Ministry of Internal Affairs to their own liking and to the circumstances in which they were operating, they continued doing so throughout 1992 and indeed on -- into 1993. Since the special units were mentioned and the previous paragraph about the transformation of the special units of the police were referred to, I just want to supplement very briefly my answer yesterday in which I was asked why -- whether there were any discussions going on in the Assembly or in the Presidency that could shed light on why there was a perceived need to restructure the Special Police unit. And I, in reacquainting myself with this report, which I wrote many years ago, note that in the section on the Special Police forces, I refer in a footnote to Radovan Karadzic's complaint that officials in municipalities throughout the RS were often behaving as I believe he calls them little princes, and again, as I noted, this included creating an atmosphere in which virtually everyone who felt like it could form a Special Police unit or form a police unit and call it special, and this had created an unenviable organisation from the perspective of the police and eventually also from the perspective of the government and the Presidency, and they took together with the Ministry of Internal Affairs decisive steps to shut down these units in a number of municipalities and in most cases restructure them into the Special Brigade of the police, to which I refer in my -- again in my report in a section on the Special Brigade of the police and CSB Special Police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Nielsen, I don't have any other questions for you at this time. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon -- good morning, Mr. Nielsen. My name is Slobodan Zecevic. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, by training you are a historian, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood well from your CV attached to the report, you were employed at the OTP as an analytics officer in charge of research in 2002 through 2004, and you worked in the section of the Office of the Prosecutor that dealt with cases against leaders; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My official title was research officer and I worked from 2002 through 2004, August of 2004, for the leadership research team; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say researching the leadership, you mean researches for the cases against Izetbegovic, Tudjman, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Milosevic? Are these the cases you mean?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the cases that were researched by members of that team; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That section of the Prosecutor, this leadership research team, is it divided internally by cases, like the Krajisnik team, Milosevic team, Tudjman team?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team was divided internally. However, this division was not on a case basis, but was, rather, divided into sub-units. There was a demographic unit, there was a Bosnian Croat unit, there was a Bosnian Serb unit, et cetera, so covering all of the leaderships that are dealt with at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose you were part of the Bosnian Serb unit; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did research both for that sub-unit of the team and also for the unit that dealt with the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means that you dealt primarily with Krajisnik, Karadzic, and Milosevic cases; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on those three cases, but I also worked extensively on other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did these other cases concern leadership or something else? Would that include this case, for instance?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I produced analytical reports primarily on the RS Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Belgrade and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia and that means that I always conduct my research based on my subject focus, the subjects being those that I just mentioned, and obviously those subjects are germane to an enormous range of cases that have been tried at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that from the moment when you joined the Prosecution, you immediately got the task to prepare such an analytical report concerning the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Because of my past research which had been focused on the police in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, I came in with experience on that issue, and there was a perceived gap at that point in time in which a report needed to be written on the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and I was asked to prepare such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Nielsen, were you informed then, were you advised for which case you were preparing that report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as indicated by the cover page of my report, it was a report prepared for the case of Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So I suppose that the instructions to make that report were given you by one the Prosecutors involved in the Krajisnik team?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I was instructed to write that report by my team leader, who was the leader of the leadership research team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after you made that report, you submitted it, I suppose, to your team leader, and he then presented it to the trial attorneys on the Prosecution side in the Krajisnik case, and then it was decided that your report should become an expert report, the expert report to be used in Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was also sent to a number of teams, both analytical and investigative teams, which were engaged in cases that also involved aspects of RS MUP, so not just to the Prosecution in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when your report was made available to all the teams that were dealing with various cases in the Office of the Prosecutor, did you receive any feedback from them in terms of suggestions or questions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the months that followed, I did receive a number of questions regarding points in the report, a point where I was asked to clarify something that I had put in because it was perceived that it was maybe not clear, questions of the nature that are being posed in this Trial Chamber today. I did receive such questions, yes, but I did not receive any suggestions in terms of how to modify the report. It was understood by all concerned that I was continuing to work on the report, and I indeed subsequently filed, I believe, already before my testimony in Krajisnik in 2005 an addendum to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that none of the teams who received your report made any suggestions to delve deeper into the subject that was important to their theory of the case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They posed questions regarding the content of the report, but they did not make suggestions to conduct further analysis that was important to their theory of the case, as you ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me be more specific. That initial report that you provided, did it contain the sub-items that it contains now, such as paragraph 1, the fragmentation of the SUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina November 1990 to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's slightly difficult for me to reconstruct, given that I don't have the original version of the report in front of me, which of the headings in the table of contents were present in the original one, and it is quite possible that I added additional headings after I filed the initial version of the report. However, all of the headings that are in this report are my headings. I'm the sole author of those headings, and no suggestions were ever made to me by anyone that I should change the wording in those headings or add specific headings or subtract or delete specific headings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to follow you, Mr. Nielsen, when you are giving such long answers. If I understood correctly, you can't remember whether the first was divided into the same number of items as this one, but you allow the possibility that some of the items were added in your follow-up work on the report. I asked you specifically about the fragmentation of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- sorry, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if that particular section was not part of your initial report, how did it come about that you eventually added that section? Was it your own idea or was it suggested to you by someone or was it asked in the form of a question?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for that question. On that specific point, I'm happy to answer that that original point under Roman numeral I was indeed in the original version of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I took that first section, that first chapter only as an example, not because I was trying to demonstrate anything in particular. I used it just as an example. Can you tell me how particular sections were created based on your ideas only or based also on some suggestions you might have received from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the sections in this report came into being the same way, the sections in my doctoral dissertation or the articles that I write came into being, that is, they come as -- on an ongoing bases as I continue to review and analyse documents, but they certainly were created based on my ideas only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What measures were taken by the Prosecution from the moment when it was decided that you would be their expert in terms of ensuring that you remain objective?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that any specific extraordinary measures were taken on that point. It was my understanding that my work and my reason for being in analytical team and working constantly under the supervision of the chief research officer who was the chief of the research leadership team was, in large part, designed to ensure that objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, the Prosecution decided to use you as their expert, to use the report that you prepared and worked on and supplemented as their expert report while you continued to work as an analyst in the Office of the Prosecutor in the leadership research team; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From 2004 to date you are an advisor analyst, a consulting analyst; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that from my departure the first time in August 2004 to the present date there were several periods in which I didn't do any consulting analysis for the OTP, but I have resumed doing consulting analysis for the OTP with specific relation to previous expert reports that I produced after I began teaching in Denmark in 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, as a consultant, you would get a question or a request from time to time from the Prosecution and in response you would provide a report or advice, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the best example would be that I was asked to produce an updated version of my expert report for the case of Stanisic Simatovic, and I was provided with documents that had been obtained since I left the OTP, and I proceeded using the same methodology as I previously described to use such an addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you get the same kind of request or instruction for this case, Stanisic and Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latest work that I did on this report was work done in January 2008, which involved reviewing a number of documents that had arrived at the OTP after I was no longer working on RS MUP, and I was asked to review those documents and, if necessary, if I thought that they shed additional analytical light on any of the topics dealt with in the report, then I was given the opportunity to amend the report accordingly. That's the last work I did on this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, you said yesterday that you not only authored the report, but that you selected alone all the documents that support your conclusions in the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Sometimes I was shown documents by my colleagues working on the military, the Crisis Staffs, or other subjects that they believed to be relevant to my research, but at the end of the day I was the sole arbiter of what documents were cited in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you also come across documents that do not support the Prosecution case in this particular trial, and if you did, did you inform the Prosecution about the existence of such documents?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My awareness of the Prosecution's theory in this case is based on my reading of the publicly available indictment of -- that or, I would say, the several indictments since there's been consolidation and revision in this case. If I came across documents which I believed to be of a potentially exonerating nature, then certainly I would raise the awareness of the Prosecution to the existence of those documents and point out that I thought that they were potentially exonerating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You must have also read the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, it's a public document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never actually read that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not even the initial one from 2004, 2005, the initial pretrial brief?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe I'd have to be provided with a date on that one, but I think that might have been made final after I left in August 2004, but I certainly haven't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will give you the date as soon as my colleagues find it. When you would come across these documents that you informed the Prosecution are potentially 68 or perhaps do not fit their theory the case as far as you were aware, did you refer to them in your report anywhere?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the subjects that I deal with and which are laid out in the table of contents, my aim was to present as complete as possible a picture as I could based on the documents available. So when I became aware of documents that contradicted points that were in earlier drafts of the report, then I certainly changed the report to take that new information into consideration, as one does when, for example, writing a work of history.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then that document would be cited in the revised footnote; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with a caveat that this is a document which presents the structure and functioning of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and illustrates based on analytical conclusions the general thrust of the operation and establishment of that ministry. When there were significant document that I thought pointed in a different direction, then I, as a rule, tried to cite them in a footnote. However, just as I cannot cite every document that supports the conclusions, I have not been able to cite every document that does not support a conclusion. That would simply involve citing a nearly infinite number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that your colleagues who worked on other aspects of this case would provide you with documents that might be interesting for you. And today on page 9, line 21 in response to a question from Mr. Hannis, you said you agreed with the findings of the report of Ms. Hanson concerning Crisis Staffs, that means that you read her report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read her report, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We heard today that in this case you also read the interview of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it and I've also had the ability to view it, yes, on video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Hanson [as interpreted], you also read some statements of witnesses, Prosecution witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have had the opportunity to read at an earlier date a very small number of statements of Prosecution witnesses. I'm more familiar with their actual statements to date in this court as I have been, to the best of my ability, following this case by reading the publicly available transcripts on the web site. I would also like to note, just to put a bit of context on it, I was provided with the interview of Mr. Stanisic and had the opportunity to review that in November, so it's very recently that I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say you are more familiar with the statements to date in this court, you mean our case, right, this case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's the transcripts that I'm reading that are on the ICTY's website.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, Mr. Hansen [as interpreted], that in the course of your work in the Office of the Prosecutor, you were also involved in taking some witness statements in this case, at least you were present?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just wanted to bring the attention to the transcript, I believe he addressed the witness as Mr. Hansen instead of Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand Scandinavian names can be confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is actually the fact that we are having expert after expert, so that it why. I'm sorry for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe this is the subconscious of my learned friend, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you would be kind to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the period from June 2002 to August 2004 I participated in a number of witness interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, then I have to ask you, bearing in mind all your previous answers, how is it that in your view you can still be an objective expert for particular issues in this case, and how you can be of assistance to the Trial Chamber with the particular knowledge that you have, while still maintaining an objective view?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. I think it's argumentative. It really goes to an issue for you to decide whether he is an objective expert or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Nielsen, let us move on to your report. Chapter number 1 is the fragmentation of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, November 1990 to April 1992. When you say November 1990, you took that date probably because that was the date of the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For this period, November 1990 to April 1992, you will agree with me, won't you, that one of the features of this period was an attempt by SDS [as interpreted] and HDZ to achieve a majority rule of a kind within the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I am sorry. For the transcript, line 3 on page 28 it should be SDA and HDZ instead of SDS.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The focus of my report is primarily on the police organs, the organs of Internal Affairs in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not an expert on the political situation during that period, and I would defer on general descriptions of that period and of the intentions of the three parties mentioned to the expert report of my colleague and boss Pat Treanor who wrote a report on the political situation during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pat Treanor, his report and his testimony were not actually used by the Prosecution, so I have to ask you, I specifically asked you about the Ministry of the Interior, I didn't ask you about the general political situation. I asked you whether one of the characteristics of that period was precisely this attempt to achieve majority rule by the members of the SDA and the HDZ within the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I mean, would you agree with me or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that this is a period in which there is, as I state, in the executive summary of the report and in the first section of the report a very tense, an increasingly tense political situation in which all three parties, as I stated yesterday, are involved in politicising the Ministry of Internal Affairs. And I would also agree, as I state in paragraph 26 my executive summary, that this increased frictions. And I also agree that from the Bosnian Serb perspective, they believed, and employees of Serb ethnicity in the SR BH MUP, believed that the SDA and the HDZ were trying to achieve dominance within the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 29, 4, I think that you said -- all right. Thank you very much. Mr. Nielsen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Footnote 18 in document 65 ter 2746, can we please look at that on our screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wish to state for the record that the reason I want to use the documents in the binder is that the screen is so blurry, I can hardly read the documents on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is your paragraph 11 on page 11 of the English version. This is a dispatch of the 19th of September, 1991, from Mr. Zupljanin, sent to the public security station in Prijedor to the chief there, and Mr. Zupljanin expresses --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see Mr. Hannis is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure the witness is following where you are. I think your reference was to paragraph 11 in his report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. Paragraph 11 of his report and the footnote 18 of his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I'm not sure he has in his binder the specific document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to look at the actual document if a hard copy to be provided or if it's in the binders, if there's a tab number I could look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not in the hard copy of the binders that I provided to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the problem is that the B/C/S, in particular ending which, in fact, is quite blurry. It makes it quite difficult for me to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have a hard copy, and we can try during the break to print the documents so that the witness could use them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, I only have the documents in the Serbian, but I assume that that would not be a difficulty for you. Do you see the document? This is, as I said, a dispatch by Mr. Zupljanin to the Prijedor SJB where Mr. Zupljanin voices his surprise and protest because legal provisions are not being taken into account while employing candidates, and to make it even more strange, four candidates, who did not pass the most elementary security clearance and so on, began to work without the agreement of the chief of the CSB. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that this document proves this tendency, which I referred to earlier, the attempt to establish a majority rule by the Muslim and Croat people in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and from what we can see here, this is even in violation of elementary laws and regulations and requirements?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with you that it proves the tendency of "majori zacija" of establishing majority rule, as it's being translated here, by the Muslim and Croat people in the MUP. I think it is an excellent illustration of a deplorable situation that obtains in SR BiH MUP from November 1990 to April 1992 where all three sides are in the habit occasionally and increasingly of proposing candidates who have not gone through the proper procedures to be employed in the organs of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see the time, Your Honours. Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume at 12.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have prepared a copy -- the hard copy of certain documents for the benefit of the witness. I showed it to my colleague and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Welcome. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the previous document, 65 ter 2746, into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 2746 shall be given Exhibit 1D112. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, the next document that I would like to discuss with you is precisely the document that you are looking at now. This is 65 ter 1798. This is a document which is an agreement on the criteria for the distribution of municipal functions and departments among the party representatives of the SDS, SDA, and the HDZ. It's a two-page document, dated the 22nd of December, 1990. The copy that we have is not signed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Stjepan Kljujic, the respective leaders of the three parties, but you will agree with me that this inter-party agreement and the criteria were actually laid down among the two -- the three parties following the elections in November 1990?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We can see on the first page of the document, for example, in item 5, this is a percentage from 33 to 50 per cent. It says: "The party which won more votes has precedence in choosing between the post of the Municipal Assembly president and that of the president of the executive committee, while the principle governing the distribution of the departments is that the first can choose first, the second second." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the following page where the criteria for the distribution of municipal functions and departments in the case of divisions among the three parties, we can see on the first page the percentage ranging from 11 to 16 per cent, and it says vice-presidential post, and it says one professional meaning that he is actually paid, and one department. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under item 5, over 25 per cent the principle for selection would be the first, according to the votes, selects first, the second second, and the third third. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you reviewed the documents, do you have any reason to doubt that these criteria agreed upon among the parties were not implemented after the 22nd of December, 1990?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly have no doubts that they were initially implemented in the form that we see it here in this particular document and in the form in which I refer to in paragraph 7 of my report for the division of functions at the top of the ministry. However, as I point out in my report, this very nice mathematical compromise, if you will, in practice quickly deteriorated with all sides accusing -- or each side accusing the other two sides of not respecting the criteria that were agreed upon, as we see in this document, or for, let's say, respecting the criteria, but appointing or nominating people who lacked the correct professional qualifications. I think that's why the word "professional" is also significant in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, I disagree with you. I think that if you look at the document under item 1 it says less than 5 per cent, one vice-presidential post on a voluntary basis, I take that to mean that it's an agreement among the parties that the party that has less than 5 per cent of the vote has the right to one vice-presidential post but this is not a paid post, the person would volunteer as a vice-president of a certain organ in the municipality. Where it says professional, in that case those posts are salaried posts. We are not talking here about whether somebody is a professional employee or not, it's just a question of whether they are actually paid for their work or not. Would you agree with me or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that. I think I was jumping a bit ahead of myself in moving to the police, whereas these are just municipal functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, unless there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 01798 shall be given Exhibit 1D113. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The next document is the one that is next in sequence in your binder. This is document 65 ter 1797, which actually goes into the specifics of what you are actually discussing in paragraph 7 of your report. This is a document from January 1991, as it is handwritten in the upper right-hand corner of the document. This is probably a copy obtained from the party premises of the Serbian Democratic Party since only candidates of the Serbian Democratic Party are mentioned here by name in this document. I would like to show it to you, though, because of what is under item 2 in that document. It refers to the Ministry of the Interior, and next to the typed posts in the ministry there is a dash after which the post is assigned to a particular party. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that this is more or less something that absolutely corresponds with what you also state in your paragraph 7, the minister is a member of the Party for Democratic Action, that is Mr. Delimustafic; the deputies from the SDS party, Vitomir Zepinic; and then the undersecretary is Mr. Kvesic [realtime transcript read in error "Kresic"] from the HDZ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph 2, could you please look next to the letter L where it says deputy of the undersecretary -- I apologise. I am being warned, on page 35, 8 it is not "Mr. Kresic" but it is "Kvesic," Branko Kvesic, with a V, from the HDZ. Now it is Kesic but it should be Kvesic, K-v-e-s-i-c. All right. I'm actually sure that this will be corrected. My question was, if you see under the letter L where it states deputy of the undersecretary for state security services, and then there is a dash, and after that it says SDS; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that that means that that post was assigned pursuant to this agreement to the party -- to the Serbian Democratic Party, SDS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then it also says Boro Susic if I'm not mistaken in the next line?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the way I read the name as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And we can see that in the document letters N and J have been added by hand and then you have two advisors, public security, and then we have the letters SDA and that is for the state security?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Although, the letters SDA are after the chief of the centre for education, training centre, and NJ, I think there was a transcript issue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, that is the next entry, under the letters NJ, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I'm again getting ahead of myself; correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no objection, I would like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I have an objection. There's not a date, and we don't know who wrote these handwritten entries on there. If it's being offered just to show that these were the positions and how they were divided between the parties, I don't disagree with that because I think it is -- it accurately represents how they were divided as I understood, so if it's being offered for that limited purposes, I don't object.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Hannis, you will have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see I'm in the transcript. My objection was that we don't have a date and we don't know who made the handwritten entries on this document. However, if the Defence is offering it for the limited purposes of showing how certain positions were divided among the parties, I don't disagree because to the best of my knowledge this does accurately reflect how they were divided at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that the witness confirmed that as far as the Ministry of the Interior is concerned, which is the only one relevant here for the purposes of this case, corresponds to the findings of the expert in item 7 of his report. I don't know in what sense does Mr. Hannis think that we are limiting the use of this document. According to everything that we know and have in the document so far from other sources, it absolutely corresponds to what the situation was in January 1991 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friends and to the others in the proceedings. I would like to put on the record that I object to the form of my learned friend Mr. Hannis' objection. He said on page 36, line 23 that -- I am a quoting, "that we don't have a date and we don't know who made the handwritten entries." Your Honours, we've been through all these matters. We have well-established practice, we have guide-lines with regard to the elements of certain documents which are required to be admitted. If our learned friend from the OTP have a certain doubt or any kind of objection, they are free to submit the request for a chain of custody and all the other stuff. We are wasting time with this particular portions, date, handwriting entries, et cetera, et cetera. We have well-established practice and we have guide-lines. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 01797 shall be given Exhibit 1D114. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the last document from this set of documents that I would like to show you is 1D01-0868.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the third document in sequence in your binder. I see that you already have it, Mr. Nielsen. This is also a draft and it's called the inter-party agreement regarding the functions in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 1D01-0868.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see what I have just read and we have the public security centres here that are listed, in all there are ten of them; is that correct, Mr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then next to the name of the centre we have Banja Luka under number one followed by Sarajevo, Tuzla, to the right-hand side it is listed which party is putting forward their candidate for chief, and then we have public security department and the state security departments next to that; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. I do see, however, and I do want to make sure we are being very precise with the terminology here, these are not actually ten public security centres. These are nine centres of security services, that includes public and state security and the Sarajevo city SUP which had a specific status under the then Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, can you please tell me since you dealt with this topic, are all the nine public security services that existed at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina listed here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and I list them in paragraph 8 of my report, and I also cite this document in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you also referred to the document, I hope it will not be a problem to have this document tendered into evidence, but I would like you to come just to two more things. From this we can see that the SDS [as interpreted] party appointed candidates of Serbian ethnicity for the posts of chief of the public security centres in four locations, the SDS also in four locations, including the city of Sarajevo, and the HDZ did the same in two locations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And I do note that there are some hand-marked changes to this. From -- for example, for Doboj we see that public security was initially listed as SDS, it's been changed in the handwriting to HDZ, I'm -- I have to say that I'm unable to say what the final outcome of this was, but it reflects the ongoing negotiations and the political situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being told that on page 39, line 6, it's SDS instead of SDA. I was talking about the democratic action party, the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, again, it says further division of staff within the centre would be based on -- would observe national proportion and would be carried out in agreement with the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that consistent with the information and the conclusions that you reached in your work?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And I note that in very faint handwriting on the -- in the original document, the relative percentages that have been agreed, including 35 point -- I believe it says 64 or 67 for the SDS, is listed it at the bottom, that is in fact also a figure to which I refer because Mr. Karadzic himself used it and that's cited in my report. So, yes, I concur.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So these percentages seem to show that according to this inter-party agreement in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the SDA would get just over 42 per cent, the SDS 35, and the rest to HDZ?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and I note that I cite that number for the SDS in paragraph 15 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no objection from my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document ID 01-0868 shall be given Exhibit 1D115. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your report you confirmed that after a while this agreement that had been reached in this way ceased to be observed; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that I indicate in my report that there were an increasing number violations of this agreement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Nielsen, that even back in March 1992, the issue and the problem about appointing the deputy secretary for the state security service in the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina remained outstanding, and according to this agreement, that post was to go to the SDS? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I note in my report that the Bosnian Serbs in the Ministry of Internal Affairs, as well as the SDS, were consistently dissatisfied with the situation in the state security service in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To illustrate that, could you please turn to 65 ter 1802. That's the next document. 65 ter 1802. It's a communique by the leading Serb employees in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina 65 ter 1802.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted the document from 9 September 1991. Right, I need page 3. The problem seems to be that this document is stapled and was put on the 65 ter list under number 1802, and actually it has nothing to do with the first two pages. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you cite it in your footnote 37, this document is dated, as I said, 9 September 1991. It was a fax sent to the Ministry of Information of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's a communique of leading Serb employees in the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and as you state, I cite it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And now in paragraph 2, the most prominent examples are cited from the past experience of the MUP, examples of violations of laws and regulations regulating security services; namely, first point, bypassing the MUP deputy minister who is an SDS member in staffing matches; two, abolishing the position of deputy undersecretary of the state security service which was to go to the SDS, according to the inter-party agreement. That's precisely what we discussed a moment ago; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then they cite inconsistent and incorrect staffing policies wherein some Serbs are being dismissed from senior positions, then a large number of people taken into the service although they have a criminal record and criminal proceedings are ongoing against them, then issuing official identity cards to persons who were are not employees of the MUP. Since you cited this document in your report, Mr. Nielsen, you will probably agree with me that these objections voiced by leading Serb employees in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina are in fact based on facts, on actual things that were happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, as I state in the report, I believe this document accurately reflects the views of leading employees of Serb nationality of MUP of BiH as to what was ongoing at that time. And I would note also the important reference to servile Serbs that I also note in paragraph 22 of my report; in other words, Serbs who did not enjoy the active support of the Serbian Democratic Party. And I would also refer the Court to footnote 39 which I believe is in the following paragraph in my report, paragraph 23, in which the SDA ironically or, I think, relevantly sends a similar complaint to Izetbegovic at the same time complaining that the Serbs were doing similar things. So again, I think I absolutely agree with you, this is what this document says. I think it's highly relevant that on certainly both the Muslim and the Serbian side such accusations were taking place with increasing frequency during this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, did I correctly hear you to use the adjective "servile" because the transcript at line 14, page 42, says "vile." Did I hear you say "servile Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you were correct in hearing me say "servile Serbs." In the original "postlusni Serbi" [phoen], and that is reflected in paragraph 22 of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if there is no objection, I would kindly ask that this document to be admitted into evidence with the proviso -- thank you, Mr. Hannis. With a proviso that, Your Honours, the first two pages of the document are not related by date or any other indicator to this document. Perhaps we should reload it into e-court under a certain separate number and then accord it an exhibit number. I don't know if Mr. Hannis has any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no objection. I have to review and see what the other two pages relate to and if that's something that we need to keep a number for, but I have no problem with the suggested procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Having regard to what Mr. Hannis has just said, I'm not sure what the suggested procedure is, that it remain as it is or that it be reloaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Registry suggested it be marked for identification at this stage, and then if the first two pages need not be removed, then it will be assigned its exhibit number, but the onus would be on counsel to remind us that it's an MFI document which has to be given an exhibit number. It's -- so the only practical question remains as to whether it's the one page or the three pages that would, in fact, be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to suggest precisely the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record 65 ter 01802 shall be given Exhibit 1D116 marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, our next document is 65 ter 37, and that is a letter of the 6th February 1992 from SDS signed by Radovan Karadzic. I think it's your footnote 76 where you considered this document. It is evident from the document that Mr. Karadzic again voices his disapproval and raises the issue of staffing in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I just want to note that I saw that I -- my previous comment about, in answering Your Honours's question about the placement of that phrase, it said in the transcript that it was in paragraph 226 of my report, paragraph 22 of the report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Nielsen, that here in para 1, Mr. Karadzic points out and demands that all appointments in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that concern the employment of around 14.00 people outside of the job specification be rendered null and void, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what the document says.
